items.followUp: Why do halogens tend to gain an electron rather than lose one?

rubric.why: Halogens have seven outer-shell electrons and can complete their octet by gaining one electron.
rubric.description: States the halogen’s outer-shell arrangement and its tendency to gain an electron.
rubric.how: Award for identifying seven outer-shell electrons and the gain of one electron.

rubric.why: The strong attraction between the nucleus and the electrons makes removing an electron require considerable energy.
rubric.description: Explains why removing an electron from a halogen is difficult.
rubric.how: Award for linking strong attraction or the considerable energy required with electron removal.

modelAnswer: A halogen atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell and tends to gain one electron to complete its octet.
The strong nuclear attraction holds its outer electrons, so removing an electron requires considerable energy.

items.followUp: State two physical properties of water that are affected by hydrogen bonding.

rubric.why: Additional energy is needed to overcome intermolecular hydrogen bonds, raising the boiling point or melting point.
rubric.description: Identifies an increase in boiling point or melting point due to hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award for stating that hydrogen bonding increases either the boiling point or melting point.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding strengthens attraction between molecules and can increase viscosity and surface tension.
rubric.description: Identifies an increase in another physical property due to hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award for stating that hydrogen bonding increases viscosity or surface tension.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding increases the boiling point and melting point because extra energy is needed to separate the molecules.
It also increases viscosity and surface tension.
